q: According to VSEPR theory, the shape of a BeCl₂ molecule is:
x: Be has two bond pairs and no lone pair, so the pairs lie on opposite sides of Be at 180°, giving a linear molecule.

q: The F–B–F bond angle in a BF₃ molecule is:
x: Boron has three bond pairs and no lone pair. They spread out in one plane at 120°, giving a trigonal planar molecule.

q: According to VSEPR theory, the strongest repulsion is between:
o: A lone pair and a bond pair
A bond pair and an inner-shell electron pair
x: The order of repulsion is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. Lone pairs are held by only one nucleus, so they spread out more and repel more strongly.

q: The H–O–H bond angle in water (104.5°) is smaller than the H–C–H angle in methane (109.5°) because:
o: The two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bond pairs more strongly and push them closer
Oxygen is less electronegative than carbon
O–H bonds are much longer than C–H bonds
x: Both have four electron pairs around the central atom, but oxygen has two lone pairs. Lone pair repulsion is stronger than bond pair repulsion, so the O–H bond pairs are squeezed to 104.5°.

q: Which description of the PCl₅ molecule is correct?
o: Square pyramidal with all bond angles 90°
Trigonal bipyramidal with bond angles of 120° and 90°
Trigonal bipyramidal with all bond angles 120°
x: P has five bond pairs and no lone pair. Three Cl atoms lie in a plane at 120° and two lie above and below that plane at 90° to it, giving a trigonal bipyramid.

q: The shape of the SF₆ molecule is:
x: Sulphur has six bond pairs and no lone pair. Six pairs are farthest apart at the corners of an octahedron, with all F–S–F angles of 90°.

q: The correct order of bond angles is:
x: All three have four electron pairs. CH₄ has no lone pair (109.5°), NH₃ has one (107°) and H₂O has two (104.5°). More lone pairs squeeze the bond angle more.

q: Which pair of species has the same bond angle?
x: CH₄ and NH₄⁺ both have four bond pairs and no lone pair on the central atom, so both are regular tetrahedra with 109.5° angles. NH₃ (107°) and H₂O (104.5°) differ because of their lone pairs.

q: Which statement about VSEPR theory is correct?
o: Valence-shell electron pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible
Lone pairs occupy less space than bond pairs
A double bond counts as two separate regions when deciding shape
Inner-shell electrons decide the shape of a molecule
x: VSEPR theory says the electron pairs in the valence shell of the central atom repel each other and take up positions as far apart as possible. A multiple bond counts as one region, and lone pairs take up more space than bond pairs.

q: The bond angle in NH₃ is 107°, but in BF₃ it is 120°. The reason for this difference is that:
o: Fluorine atoms are larger than hydrogen atoms
Boron is more electronegative than nitrogen
Nitrogen has four electron pairs including a lone pair, while boron has only three bond pairs
NH₃ contains a pi bond and BF₃ does not
x: N in NH₃ has three bond pairs and one lone pair, arranged roughly tetrahedrally, so the molecule is pyramidal with 107°. B in BF₃ has only three bond pairs, which spread out in a plane at 120°.

q: In a methane (CH₄) molecule, the four hydrogen atoms lie at the corners of a:
x: Carbon has four bond pairs and no lone pair. Four pairs are farthest apart when pointing to the corners of a regular tetrahedron, with H–C–H angles of 109.5°.

q: A sigma (σ) bond is formed by:
o: Sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals
Head-on (end-to-end) overlap of orbitals along the line joining the nuclei
Complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another
Overlap of two completely filled orbitals
x: A sigma bond forms by head-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis. Sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals gives a pi bond, and electron transfer gives an ionic bond.

q: How many sigma and pi bonds are present in one molecule of ethene, CH₂=CH₂?
x: There are four C–H sigma bonds, and the C=C double bond has one sigma and one pi bond. Total: 5 sigma and 1 pi.

q: How many sigma and pi bonds are present in one molecule of ethyne, HC≡CH?
x: There are two C–H sigma bonds, and the C≡C triple bond has one sigma and two pi bonds. Total: 3 sigma and 2 pi.

q: Which statement about a pi (π) bond is correct?
o: Its electron density lies above and below the line joining the nuclei
It can be formed by overlap of two s orbitals
It is formed before the sigma bond between two atoms
It allows free rotation of the bonded atoms
x: A pi bond comes from sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, so its electron cloud lies above and below the internuclear axis. s orbitals cannot form pi bonds, a pi bond only forms after a sigma bond, and it prevents rotation.

q: There is no free rotation about the C=C double bond in ethene because:
o: The sigma bond is broken by any rotation
The two carbon atoms are sp³ hybridised
Rotation would destroy the sideways overlap of the p orbitals forming the pi bond
The C=C bond contains two sigma bonds
x: The pi bond needs the two p orbitals to stay parallel. Twisting one carbon would break that sideways overlap, so rotation is restricted. A sigma bond alone is symmetrical about the axis and allows rotation.

q: A sigma bond between two carbon atoms is stronger than a pi bond between them because:
o: A sigma bond contains more electrons than a pi bond
The extent of orbital overlap is greater in head-on overlap
A pi bond is formed from s orbitals
A sigma bond is formed by sideways overlap
x: Head-on overlap concentrates electron density directly between the nuclei and gives greater overlap than sideways overlap. Both bonds hold two electrons, so strength depends on the extent of overlap.

q: How many sigma and pi bonds are present in one molecule of benzene, C₆H₆?
x: Benzene has six C–C sigma bonds and six C–H sigma bonds (12 sigma), plus three pi bonds from the three C=C double bonds of the Kekulé structure. Total: 12 sigma and 3 pi.

q: How many sigma and pi bonds are present in a molecule of carbon dioxide, O=C=O?
x: Each C=O double bond has one sigma and one pi bond. With two double bonds, CO₂ has 2 sigma and 2 pi bonds.

q: Which type of orbital overlap gives a pi bond?
o: Head-on overlap of an s orbital and a p orbital
Sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals
Head-on overlap of two p orbitals along the bond axis
x: Only sideways (lateral) overlap of parallel p orbitals gives a pi bond. s–s, s–p and head-on p–p overlaps all lie along the bond axis and give sigma bonds.

q: Which statement about a triple bond between two atoms is correct?
o: It consists of three sigma bonds
It consists of two sigma bonds and one pi bond
It consists of one sigma bond and two pi bonds lying in the same plane
It consists of one sigma bond and two pi bonds lying at right angles to each other
x: Only one sigma bond can form between two atoms. The other two bonds are pi bonds from two pairs of p orbitals (for example py and pz) that are perpendicular, so the two pi clouds are at right angles.

q: The hybridisation of the carbon atom in methane (CH₄) is:
x: Carbon mixes its 2s and three 2p orbitals to form four equal sp³ hybrid orbitals, which point to the corners of a tetrahedron and overlap with hydrogen 1s orbitals.

q: In BeCl₂, the beryllium atom is:
o: sp³ hybridised and the molecule is tetrahedral
sp² hybridised and the molecule is trigonal planar
sp hybridised and the molecule is bent
sp hybridised and the molecule is linear
x: Be mixes one 2s and one 2p orbital to give two sp hybrid orbitals at 180°. Each overlaps with a Cl orbital, so BeCl₂ is linear.

q: The percentage of s character in an sp² hybrid orbital is:
x: An sp² orbital is made from one s and two p orbitals, so it is one-third s: 33.3%. sp³ has 25% s character and sp has 50%.

q: In ethene (CH₂=CH₂), the pi bond between the two carbon atoms is formed by overlap of:
o: An sp² hybrid orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
x: Each carbon in ethene is sp² hybridised and keeps one unhybridised 2p orbital. These two p orbitals overlap sideways to form the pi bond. sp²–sp² overlap gives the C–C sigma bond.

q: Which option correctly gives the hybridisation of nitrogen in NH₃ and the shape of the molecule?
x: N forms four sp³ hybrid orbitals: three bond to H and one holds a lone pair. The electron pairs are roughly tetrahedral, but the molecular shape (atoms only) is pyramidal.

q: In which molecule is the central atom sp² hybridised?
x: Boron in BF₃ mixes one 2s and two 2p orbitals to form three sp² orbitals at 120°. Carbon in CH₄ and nitrogen in NH₃ are sp³, and Be in BeCl₂ is sp.

q: In propene, CH₃–CH=CH₂, the hybridisation of the three carbon atoms from left to right is:
x: The CH₃ carbon has four single bonds, so it is sp³. The two carbons joined by the double bond each have three sigma bonds and one pi bond, so both are sp².

q: Which pair correctly matches a hybridisation with the angle between its hybrid orbitals?
x: sp³ orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5°. sp orbitals are at 180° and sp² orbitals are at 120°.

q: In a water molecule, how many of the four sp³ hybrid orbitals of oxygen contain lone pairs?
x: Oxygen has six valence electrons. Two sp³ orbitals hold one electron each and bond to H; the other two hold lone pairs. This is why water is bent.

q: The C–H bond in ethyne (HC≡CH) is shorter than the C–H bond in ethane because the carbon orbital used in ethyne:
o: Has 50% s character and holds electrons closer to the nucleus
x: Ethyne carbon is sp hybridised (50% s character), while ethane carbon is sp³ (25% s). s orbitals are closer to the nucleus, so more s character gives a shorter, stronger bond.

q: A central atom with three bond pairs and no lone pair gives a molecule with the shape:
x: Three bond pairs with no lone pair spread out in one plane at 120°, giving a trigonal planar shape, as in BF₃.

q: A central atom X has three bond pairs and one lone pair in its valence shell. The shape of the molecule XY₃ is:
x: The four electron pairs point roughly to the corners of a tetrahedron. One corner is a lone pair, so the atoms form a pyramid, as in NH₃.

q: A molecule whose central atom has two bond pairs and two lone pairs has the shape:
x: Four electron pairs are arranged roughly tetrahedrally, but two are lone pairs. The three atoms therefore form a bent (V-shaped) molecule, as in H₂O.

q: The shape of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, is:
x: In NH₄⁺ the lone pair of NH₃ has formed a bond with H⁺, so N has four bond pairs and no lone pair. The ion is tetrahedral with 109.5° angles.

q: The shape of the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺, is:
x: In H₃O⁺, oxygen has three bond pairs and one remaining lone pair. Like NH₃, this gives a pyramidal shape.

q: In SO₂, sulphur has two bonding regions to oxygen and one lone pair. The shape of the SO₂ molecule is:
x: Each S–O bond region counts once, so S has three electron regions arranged roughly trigonally. One is a lone pair, so the three atoms form a bent molecule, unlike linear CO₂.

q: BCl₃ is trigonal planar, but PCl₃ is pyramidal. This is because:
o: The Cl atoms in PCl₃ are larger than those in BCl₃
Phosphorus has a lone pair in addition to its three bond pairs
Boron has a lone pair but phosphorus does not
x: B in BCl₃ has three bond pairs and no lone pair, so it is planar. P in PCl₃ has three bond pairs and one lone pair; the four pairs are tetrahedral, so the molecule is pyramidal.

q: CO₂ is a linear molecule because the carbon atom has:
o: Four bond pairs and no lone pair
Two bond pairs and two lone pairs
Two bonding regions and no lone pair
Two bonding regions and one lone pair
x: Each C=O double bond counts as one bonding region. Carbon has two regions and no lone pair, so they lie at 180° and CO₂ is linear.

q: Which molecule has the same shape as NH₃?
x: PCl₃, like NH₃, has three bond pairs and one lone pair on the central atom, so it is pyramidal. BF₃ and SO₃ are trigonal planar, and CH₄ is tetrahedral.

q: A central atom has four electron pairs, two of which are lone pairs. The approximate bond angle in the molecule is:
x: Two bond pairs and two lone pairs give a bent molecule like H₂O. The two lone pairs squeeze the bond angle from 109.5° to about 104.5°; 107° belongs to one lone pair, as in NH₃.

q: Which of the following molecules is non-polar?
x: CO₂ is linear, so its two C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. H₂O (bent), NH₃ (pyramidal) and HCl all have a net dipole moment.

q: Each C=O bond in CO₂ is polar, yet the CO₂ molecule has zero dipole moment. This is because:
o: Carbon and oxygen have the same electronegativity
The molecule is linear and the two bond dipoles cancel
The C=O bonds contain pi bonds
x: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so each bond is polar. But in the linear molecule the two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and their effects cancel.

q: Which of the following has a zero dipole moment?
x: In tetrahedral CCl₄ all four C–Cl bond dipoles are equal and symmetrically arranged, so they cancel. In the other three, unequal bonds (C–H and C–Cl) leave a net dipole.

q: BF₃ is non-polar but NH₃ is polar because:
o: B–F bonds are non-polar while N–H bonds are polar
BF₃ has a lone pair on boron
BF₃ is symmetrical and planar, while NH₃ is pyramidal with a lone pair
x: B–F bonds are polar, but in the symmetrical trigonal planar BF₃ the three dipoles cancel. NH₃ is pyramidal with a lone pair on N, so its bond dipoles do not cancel.

q: Which of the following compounds has a zero dipole moment?
x: In trans-1,2-dichloroethene the two C–Cl bonds are on opposite sides of the double bond and point in opposite directions, so their dipoles cancel. In the cis and 1,1 forms both C–Cl dipoles point the same side.

q: If the water molecule were linear like CO₂ instead of bent, its dipole moment would be:
o: Exactly the same as it is now
x: In a linear H–O–H the two equal O–H bond dipoles would point in opposite directions and cancel. Water is polar only because its bent shape stops this cancellation.

q: The dipole moment of a molecule is commonly expressed in:
x: Dipole moment is usually given in debye; in SI units it is coulomb metre (C m). A coulomb alone is a unit of charge, not of dipole moment.

q: The dipole moment (μ) of a polar bond is defined as:
o: Charge divided by the distance between the charges
Charge multiplied by the square of the distance
Charge multiplied by the distance between the charges
x: μ = q × r, the magnitude of the partial charge times the distance between the centres of positive and negative charge.

q: Which pair contains two polar molecules?
x: Bent H₂O and pyramidal NH₃ both have lone pairs and unsymmetrical shapes, so both have a dipole moment. CO₂, BF₃, CH₄ and CCl₄ are symmetrical and non-polar.

q: A triatomic molecule XY₂, in which the X–Y bonds are polar, is found to have a dipole moment. What can be concluded about its shape?
o: Its shape cannot affect its dipole moment
x: If XY₂ were linear, the two equal X–Y bond dipoles would cancel and the dipole moment would be zero. A measurable dipole moment means the molecule must be bent.

q: PCl₅ has polar P–Cl bonds, yet the PCl₅ molecule has zero dipole moment. This is because:
o: Phosphorus and chlorine have equal electronegativity
Phosphorus has a lone pair that cancels the bond dipoles
Its trigonal bipyramidal shape is symmetrical, so the bond dipoles cancel
x: PCl₅ is trigonal bipyramidal with no lone pair on P. The three equatorial dipoles cancel each other, and the two axial ones point in opposite directions, so the net dipole is zero.

q: The ionic character of a covalent bond increases as:
o: The electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms increases
The electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms decreases
The two bonded atoms become identical
The number of shared electron pairs increases
x: The larger the electronegativity difference, the more the shared pair is pulled towards one atom, and the greater the partial charges and ionic character. Identical atoms give a pure covalent bond.

q: Which bond has the greatest ionic character?
x: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so the electronegativity difference is greatest in H–F. Ionic character falls from H–F to H–I as halogen electronegativity decreases.

q: An electronegativity difference of about 1.7 between two bonded atoms corresponds to roughly:
x: By the usual rule, a difference of about 1.7 gives a bond that is about 50% ionic. Above this the bond is mainly ionic; below it, mainly covalent.

q: Which bond has no ionic character at all?
x: In Cl–Cl both atoms have the same electronegativity, so the electron pair is shared equally and the bond is purely covalent. Every bond between different atoms has some ionic character.

q: The observed dipole moment of a diatomic molecule is 1.2 D. If the bond were 100% ionic, its dipole moment would be 6.0 D. The percentage ionic character of the bond is:
x: % ionic character = (observed μ ÷ μ for 100% ionic) × 100 = (1.2 ÷ 6.0) × 100 = 20%. Dividing the other way gives 5, and 80% is the covalent part.

q: In a molecule of hydrogen chloride, the partial charges are:
o: δ+ on hydrogen and δ− on chlorine
δ+ on chlorine and δ− on hydrogen
Full positive charge on hydrogen and full negative charge on chlorine
x: Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so it pulls the shared pair closer and carries a partial negative charge (δ−); hydrogen carries δ+. The charges are partial because HCl is covalent, not ionic.

q: Which statement about a polar covalent bond is correct?
o: The electron pair is shared exactly equally
The electron pair is completely transferred to one atom
The shared pair is displaced towards the less electronegative atom
The shared pair is displaced towards the more electronegative atom
x: In a polar covalent bond the electrons are still shared, but unequally: the more electronegative atom pulls them closer and gains a partial negative charge. Complete transfer would make an ionic bond.

q: Which is the correct order of increasing ionic character?
x: Halogen electronegativity rises from I to F, so the electronegativity difference with carbon, and the ionic character, increase in the order C–I < C–Br < C–Cl < C–F.

q: Electronegativities: H 2.1, C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.5. Which bond is the most polar?
x: Differences: O–H 1.4, N–H 0.9, C–N 0.5, C–H 0.4. The largest difference, O–H, gives the most polar bond.

q: The dipole moments of the hydrogen halides decrease from HF to HI mainly because:
o: The electronegativity difference between hydrogen and the halogen decreases
The H–X bond length decreases from HF to HI
The halogens become more electronegative from F to I
The molar mass of the molecule increases
x: Electronegativity falls from F to I, so the H–X bond becomes less polar and the partial charges smaller. Bond length actually increases down the group, but the fall in charge has the bigger effect.

q: Iodine (I₂) is a non-polar molecule. It dissolves best in:
x: "Like dissolves like": non-polar I₂ dissolves in non-polar CCl₄. It is only very slightly soluble in polar water and in aqueous solutions.

q: Sodium chloride dissolves in water but not in benzene because:
o: Water molecules are polar and attract and surround the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
x: The negative (oxygen) end of water dipoles attracts Na⁺ and the positive (hydrogen) end attracts Cl⁻, pulling ions out of the lattice. Non-polar benzene cannot attract ions in this way.

q: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) mixes with water in all proportions, but hexane (C₆H₁₄) does not. This is because:
o: Hexane is polar and water is non-polar
Hexane has a lower molar mass than ethanol
Ethanol's polar O–H group can form hydrogen bonds with water, while hexane is non-polar
x: Ethanol has a polar O–H group that hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so it mixes. Hexane is non-polar and cannot attract water molecules, so the two form separate layers.

q: cis-1,2-dichloroethene boils at a higher temperature than trans-1,2-dichloroethene, although both have the same molar mass. The reason is that:
o: The cis isomer is polar and has dipole–dipole attractions, while the trans isomer is non-polar
The trans isomer forms hydrogen bonds
The cis isomer has a higher molar mass
The trans isomer has stronger dipole–dipole attractions
x: In the cis isomer the two C–Cl dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule is polar and its molecules attract each other by dipole–dipole forces. In the trans isomer they cancel, so only weaker forces act.

q: Water (H₂O) boils at 100 °C, while hydrogen sulphide (H₂S), with a larger molar mass, is a gas at room temperature. The main reason is that:
o: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds because the O–H bond is highly polar
H₂S is more polar than water
x: Oxygen is much more electronegative than sulphur, so O–H bonds are highly polar and water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds. These need extra energy to overcome, raising the boiling point.

q: The C=O bond in aldehydes and ketones is polar. As a result, the carbonyl carbon is attacked by:
o: Electrophiles, because it carries a partial negative charge
Free radicals only, because the bond is non-polar
Nucleophiles, because it carries a partial negative charge
Nucleophiles, because it carries a partial positive charge
x: Oxygen is more electronegative, so it takes δ− and the carbonyl carbon is left δ+. Electron-rich nucleophiles are attracted to this partially positive carbon.

q: The reaction between aqueous silver nitrate and aqueous sodium chloride to form a white precipitate is almost instantaneous because:
o: It involves breaking strong covalent bonds
It occurs between free ions that combine without bonds needing to be broken
It needs a catalyst to proceed
x: In water both compounds are present as free ions. Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ simply combine, so no covalent bonds have to be broken and the reaction is very fast. Reactions of covalent compounds are usually slower.

q: A charged plastic rod is held near thin streams of four liquids. Which stream will be clearly deflected?
x: Water molecules are polar, so they turn and are attracted towards the charged rod, bending the stream. Hexane, CCl₄ and benzene are non-polar and are not noticeably deflected.

q: Propanone (CH₃COCH₃) and butane (C₄H₁₀) both have molar mass 58 g mol⁻¹, but propanone boils at a much higher temperature. The main reason is that:
o: Propanone is polar, so its molecules attract by dipole–dipole forces
Propanone molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
Propanone has many more electrons than butane
x: Propanone has a polar C=O group, so its molecules attract by dipole–dipole forces; butane is non-polar. Propanone has no O–H or N–H bond, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself.

q: Sucrose (table sugar) is a covalent compound, yet it dissolves readily in water. This is because:
o: Sucrose ionises completely into ions in water
Sucrose has many polar O–H groups that form hydrogen bonds with water
x: Sucrose does not ionise, but its many O–H groups are polar and hydrogen bond with water molecules. This attraction lets the sugar molecules spread through the water.

q: Bond energy is best defined as the energy:
o: Released when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements
Needed to break one mole of a particular bond in gaseous molecules to give separate gaseous atoms
Needed to remove one electron from a gaseous atom
Released when one mole of a solid dissolves in water
x: Bond energy is the energy required to break one mole of a given bond in the gaseous state into separate atoms, in kJ mol⁻¹. The first option describes enthalpy of formation, and the second ionisation energy.

q: Which is the correct order of bond energy for carbon–carbon bonds?
x: More shared electron pairs hold the atoms more strongly. A triple bond is strongest and shortest, then a double bond, then a single bond.

q: For bonds between the same two kinds of atoms, which relationship is generally correct?
o: The longer the bond, the greater its bond energy
Bond energy does not depend on bond length
The shorter the bond, the greater its bond energy
x: Shorter bonds mean the nuclei are closer to the shared electrons, so more energy is needed to break them. For example, C≡C is shorter and stronger than C–C.

q: Which hydrogen halide has the weakest H–X bond?
x: Down the group the halogen atom gets larger, the H–X bond gets longer, and the bond energy falls. H–I is the longest and weakest, which is why HI is the strongest acid of the four.

q: Bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. What is ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)?
x: Bonds broken = 436 + 242 = 678; bonds formed = 2 × 431 = 862. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting the 2 gives +247.

q: For CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g), ΔH = +1664 kJ mol⁻¹. The average C–H bond energy is:
x: Breaking one CH₄ molecule breaks four C–H bonds, so the average C–H bond energy = 1664 ÷ 4 = 416 kJ mol⁻¹.

q: Nitrogen gas (N₂) is very unreactive at room temperature mainly because:
o: It has a very high N≡N bond energy
Its molecules contain only pi bonds
Nitrogen has a very low electronegativity
x: The N≡N triple bond (one sigma and two pi bonds) is short and very strong. A large amount of energy is needed to break it, so N₂ reacts only under harsh conditions.

q: The H–F bond energy is much greater than the average of the H–H and F–F bond energies. This extra strength is mainly due to:
o: The polarity (ionic character) of the H–F bond
The H–F bond being a double bond
The presence of a lone pair on hydrogen
The H–F bond being longer than the H–H bond
x: The large electronegativity difference gives H–F partial ionic character. The extra attraction between δ+ H and δ− F adds to the covalent bond strength, making polar bonds stronger than expected.

q: Which statement about energy changes in bonds is correct?
o: Both bond breaking and bond formation absorb energy
Both bond breaking and bond formation release energy
Bond breaking absorbs energy and bond formation releases energy
Bond breaking releases energy and bond formation absorbs energy
x: Energy must be supplied to pull bonded atoms apart, so bond breaking is endothermic. The same amount of energy is released when that bond forms, so bond formation is exothermic.

q: The F–F bond energy is lower than the Cl–Cl bond energy, even though fluorine atoms are smaller. This is mainly because:
o: The F–F bond is a pi bond
Lone pairs on the two small, close fluorine atoms repel each other strongly
Fluorine is less electronegative than chlorine
The F–F bond is longer than the Cl–Cl bond
x: The F–F bond is very short, so the lone pairs on the two fluorine atoms are close together and repel strongly, which weakens the bond. Chlorine atoms are larger, so this repulsion is much smaller.
